subject: Latent variable model with high R squares still fails X2 test

messages.author: 052329afd9841580
messages.subject: Latent variable model with high R squares still fails X2 test
parts:
Hello,

My question in brief: Is using multiple correlated exogenous variables to construct a latent variable a worthwhile exercise, or should one of these correlated variables simply be selected as an observed representation of the latent processes?


I believe the following analysis is returning low model-level P value because of strong correlations within and among two sets of exogenous variables: abiotic 'gradients' and species 'filters'. The problem arises that all correlations cannot be specified, or the model will be unidentified. A simpler model with no latent variables and a subset of the exogenous variables passes with little problem. 


The problem is particularly frustrating, because R2 values for endogenous variables are all appreciably high and the model is running with no problems in its current incarnation (though warning do arise following slight changes to causal structure). However, the P value for the overall X2 doesn’t budge, even after using modification indices to suggest new paths. Are relatively large samples size (n = 324) and degrees of freedom (~50) contributing to this low P value?  


Model:

SEM.compo<- "


#latent valiables

Filter =~  1*Hmax + SeM + WSG + LMA

Gradient =~  1*ele+ GWC + NH4 + NO3


#exogenous variances

Hmax ~~ LMA 

Hmax ~~ SeM

  Hmax ~~ WSG 

SeM ~~ LMA

SeM ~~ WSG

WSG ~~ LMA


ele ~~ GWC 

ele ~~ NH4

GWC~~ NH4

NO3 ~~ GWC 

NO3 ~~ NH4

NO3~~ ele


#Regressions

Filter~ Gradient

FDis ~ Gradient + Hmax

Nleaf ~ Gradient

Filter~~Nleaf


mean.D  ~ Nleaf + Filter + Hmax

density ~ Nleaf + Filter + Hmax

mean.D ~~ density


biomass ~ mean.D + density + Nleaf + Filter

gain  ~ mean.D + density + FDis 

biomass~~gain

"

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Latent variable model with high R squares still fails X2 test
parts:
Indicators of latent variables are endogenous, not exogenous (they are caused by the latent variable that the reflectively measure).  I'm surprised your model even runs, given that you saturate the covariances among the indicators and then still try to extract common-factor variance from them.  But from your description, it doesn't sound like a common factor model is appropriate for your data anyway.  This isn't a lavaan issue, so you should post this to SEMNET

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

You can search Google and the SEMNET boards for discussions of formative vs. reflective measurement.  If reading some articles on the topic doesn't help you form a clear picture of what you want to model, then posting a question on SEMNET should hopefully elicit some responses from a wide array of SEM experts in various fields.

Terry

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Latent variable model with high R squares still fails X2 test
parts:
Jon,
I agree that this is more of a SEMNET question than a lavaan question.

I think that what is happening is this.  You have saturated the covariances among indicators of the same LV with correlated residuals.  So, the factor model parameters are identified by the covariances between indicators of different LVs.  This is similar to a bifactor model in which each LV is like a general factor and the correlated residuals are like orthogonal specific factors with two indicators each.  The linear relationship between the LVs may not suffice to account for the pattern of covariances between indicators of different LVs.

A good place to start might be Bollen & Diamantopoulos (2015) followed by Edwards (2011).  You might also find chapters 6-8 of my book with Denny Borsboom helpful.

Once you arrive at a model that makes sense for your purposes, if something like this comes up, the matrix of correlation residuals can be very helpful in working out the problem areas in a model.  This is especially helpful in tandem with consideration of the constraints that the model places on the moment matrix.  Personally, I like to put the non-redundant residuals into a stem-and-leaf plot to evaluate outliers.  If you have a large number of saturated covariances, sometimes it can be helpful to filter out the zero residuals first.

>>>
sessionInfo()
require(lavaan)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)

# Extract residuals
implied_cov <- inspect(fit, "cov.ov")
observed_cov <- inspect(fit, "sampstat")$cov
implied_cor <- cov2cor(implied_cov)
observed_cor <- cov2cor(observed_cov)
residuals_cor <- observed_cor - implied_cor
residuals_cor

# Plot residuals
residuals_cor_unique <-
  residuals_cor[lower.tri(residuals_cor, diag=TRUE)]
stem(residuals_cor_unique)

# Plot non-zero residuals
residuals_cor_unique_nonzero <-
  residuals_cor_unique[residuals_cor_unique != 0]
stem(residuals_cor_unique_nonzero)
>>>

Good luck,
Keith
